scenes.title: Clicking vs telling: a restaurant menu
scenes.body: In a restaurant you can **point at pictures** on the menu, or you can **tell the waiter exactly** what you want: "one masala dosa, less spicy, no onion". The mouse is pointing. The terminal is telling: exact, fast, and easy to repeat.

scenes.title: rm has no Recycle Bin
scenes.body: A file deleted with `rm` is **gone**: no Trash, no undo. Read every `rm` twice, especially `rm -r`. Never paste a command you don't understand, and be extra careful with `sudo` (run as administrator).

scenes.heading: Five habits that make the terminal fast

items.text: **Tab** completes names: type `hel` + Tab → `hello.py`
items.sub: fewer typos, and it proves the file is there

items.text: **Up arrow** brings back your last commands
items.sub: edit and re-run instead of retyping

items.text: **Ctrl + C** stops a running command
items.sub: when something hangs or runs forever

items.text: `clear` (or Ctrl + L) cleans the screen
`command --help` explains any command

items.q: What is the difference between an absolute and a relative path?
items.a: An **absolute** path starts at the root (`/home/student/projects/app.py`) and works from anywhere. A **relative** path starts from the current working directory (`app.py`, `../data/x.csv`), so it depends on where you run the command.
items.trap: Code that opens `data.csv` works on your machine and fails in production because it was run from a different folder.

items.q: What does an exit code tell you?
items.a: Whether a command succeeded: **0 means success**, anything else is a failure. Scripts, CI pipelines and tools like `&&` use it to decide what runs next.
items.trap: Checking only the printed text. A program can print "done" and still fail with a non-zero code.

items.q: You type `python3` and get "command not found". What do you check?
items.a: Spelling first; then whether Python is installed; then whether its folder is on **PATH** (`which python3`, `echo $PATH`). On Windows, try `python` or `py`.
items.trap: Reinstalling everything before reading the error.
